title: Python
description: Learn Python by running small programs, practicing each concept, and building a persistent study log. Twelve lessons form a practical beginner foundation, with offline examples and self-checks.
prerequisites: Comfort creating files and opening a terminal; no programming experience required.
A computer with a current supported Python 3 interpreter.
outcomes: Run and explain short Python scripts.
Use values, collections, conditions, loops, and functions to transform data.
Validate inputs, read tracebacks, and persist records as UTF-8 JSON.
Organize modules and understand project environments.
Write small deterministic tests and distinguish API I/O from data processing.
Build and extend a local study log with explicit limitations.
setup: Install a supported Python 3 release from python.org if needed; this path uses only the standard library.
Confirm python --version (Windows may use py; macOS/Linux may use python3).
Create an empty practice folder. Save each example as a .py file and run it from that folder.
Examples show expected output as comments; the exercise starter and solution are separate snippets. Predict the result, attempt the exercise, then compare the solution.
In lesson 10 create an optional project virtual environment; no third-party packages or live API credentials are required.
nextSteps: Add an argparse command interface and regression tests to your study log.
Study classes, iterators, generators, and type hints in the official tutorial.
Choose one real API, read its authentication and rate-limit documentation, and build a separate integration test.
Learn packaging and dependency management when your project needs external libraries.

sources.title: Python tutorial: language and standard-library foundations

lessons.title: 1. Run your first program
lessons.takeaway: A program is a sequence of instructions executed by an interpreter.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Python reads your source code and performs its instructions. A script is a plain text file ending in .py. The interpreter is the program that runs it; a terminal is where you ask the interpreter to run a file.

Save the example as hello.py in a folder you can find. Open a terminal in that folder and run python hello.py. On Windows, py hello.py may work instead; on macOS or Linux the command is often python3 hello.py. Use the same interpreter command throughout this path.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: print sends a value to the terminal. Quotation marks delimit text, called a string; they do not appear in the output. Python runs these lines from top to bottom.
sections.example:
print("Hello, Python!")
print("One small step")

# Expected output:
# Hello, Python!
# One small step

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: The interactive prompt shows >>> and runs one instruction at a time. Do not copy >>> into a script. If the terminal cannot find Python, fix the installation or interpreter selection before debugging your code. A file named python.py can also shadow library imports later.

exercise.prompt: Create a greeting script that prints your name on one line and one learning goal on the next. Use the sample values below to check your version.
exercise.starter:
print("YOUR NAME")
# Print your goal next
checks: Running the script finishes without an error.
There are two lines: Asha, then Build a useful script.
Change both strings and run the file again; the output changes.

quiz.question: What runs the instructions in a .py file?
quiz.explanation: The interpreter executes Python source. The terminal gives you a way to invoke it.

lessons.title: 2. Values, variables, and numbers
lessons.takeaway: Variables name values; arithmetic produces new values.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: An assignment such as count = 3 binds a name to a value. Reading count later retrieves that value. Reassigning count changes what the name refers to; = is assignment, while == compares values.

Integers represent whole numbers, floats represent approximate fractional numbers, strings represent text, and booleans are True or False. Choose names that describe the value, such as minutes_per_day, and use type(value) when you need to inspect a type.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The example totals study time and uses an f-string to insert values into text. Division / produces a float. The // operator gives floor division, and % gives a remainder.
sections.example:
minutes_per_day = 25
days = 4
total = minutes_per_day * days
print(f"Total: {total} minutes")
print(f"Hours: {total / 60:.2f}")

# Expected output:
# Total: 100 minutes
# Hours: 1.67

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Decimal floats can have tiny representation errors: 0.1 + 0.2 need not equal 0.3 exactly. Avoid exact equality for measured fractional values; for money use integer smallest units or learn decimal.Decimal. A name is case sensitive: Minutes and minutes are different names.

exercise.prompt: Compute the cost of 3 notebooks at 125 cents each. Print total cents and a two-decimal price in dollars.
exercise.starter:
quantity = 3
unit_cents = 125
# Compute and print total
exercise.solution:
quantity = 3
unit_cents = 125
total_cents = quantity * unit_cents
print(total_cents)
print(f"${total_cents / 100:.2f}")
checks: Output is 375 then $3.75.
Changing quantity to 0 yields 0 and $0.00.
The stored total uses integer cents.

quiz.question: What does total = total + 1 do?
options: Binds total to its previous value plus 1
Creates a second variable with the same name
quiz.explanation: The right side is evaluated first, then the name on the left is assigned the resulting value.

lessons.title: 3. Text and user input
lessons.takeaway: Convert text deliberately before doing numeric work.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Strings are sequences of characters. Indexing starts at zero: name[0] is the first character. A slice such as name[:3] selects a portion. len(name) counts characters, and methods such as strip and lower return transformed strings.

input displays an optional prompt and returns a string, even when a user types digits. int converts suitable text to an integer; float converts suitable text to a floating-point number. This lesson uses fixed input text so the example runs without waiting for a person.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: Trimming surrounding spaces and normalizing case helps compare user input. The example converts the age before adding one. Try replacing raw_age with input("Age: ") after you understand the deterministic version.
sections.example:
raw_name = "  Mira  "
raw_age = "20"
name = raw_name.strip()
age = int(raw_age)
print(f"Hi {name}, next year you will be {age + 1}.")
print(name.lower())

# Expected output:
# Hi Mira, next year you will be 21.
# mira

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Strings do not change in place: name.strip() returns a value you must use or assign. int("twenty") raises ValueError; we handle this in lesson 8. Never use eval to interpret user input. Indexing an empty string fails, so inspect length before reading its first character.

exercise.prompt: Normalize the text "  PYTHON  " to lowercase without surrounding spaces, then print its length.
exercise.solution:
raw = "  PYTHON  "
clean = raw.strip().lower()
print(clean)
print(len(clean))
checks: Output is python then 6.
The original raw string still contains spaces.
Replacing raw with "  " yields an empty string and length 0.

quiz.question: What type does input return?
quiz.explanation: Input returns text. Your program decides whether and how to convert it.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A comparison returns a boolean: score >= 50 asks whether the score meets a threshold. An if block runs only when its condition is true. elif tests another condition, and else handles the remaining cases.
Indentation defines the body of a block. Use four spaces consistently. Combine conditions with and, or, and not; use parentheses when the intended grouping is not obvious.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The first matching branch wins. Test the highest threshold first here so a score of 85 does not get caught by the lower passing threshold. Predict the output before running.

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Use == to compare, not =. Separate conditions such as score >= 50 and score < 80 must each express a comparison; Python also supports 50 <= score < 80. Put boundary values in your checks because > and >= differ at exactly the threshold.

exercise.prompt: Classify a temperature: below 10 is cold, from 10 through 29 is mild, and 30 or above is hot. Start with 30.
checks: 30 prints hot.
10 prints mild; 9 prints cold.
29 prints mild, covering both boundaries.

quiz.question: If both if and elif conditions are true, which branch runs?
quiz.explanation: An if/elif/else chain selects the first condition that is true and skips the remaining branches.

lessons.title: 5. Store related values
lessons.takeaway: Choose a collection by how you need to access and change data.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A list stores an ordered sequence and can be changed with append or item assignment. A tuple is an ordered sequence whose item references cannot be reassigned. A dictionary maps unique keys to values; use meaningful keys for records such as a task title and status.

A set stores unique values and is useful for membership checks and removing duplicates. Set iteration order is not a display contract, so sort a set before producing predictable output. Dictionary indexing raises KeyError for a missing key; get supplies an optional fallback.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The list keeps task order, while the dictionary connects task names to durations. A set removes repeated tags. The copy operation matters when you want an independent list instead of another name for the same one.
sections.example:
tasks = ["read", "code"]
tasks.append("review")
minutes = {"read": 15, "code": 30}
print(tasks[1])
print(minutes.get("review", 0))
print(sorted(set(["python", "study", "python"])))

# Expected output:
# code
# 0
# ['python', 'study']

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Assigning second = first shares the same list; editing either name edits that list. Use first.copy() for a shallow copy, remembering that nested objects remain shared. {} makes an empty dictionary; set() makes an empty set. List indices start at zero.

exercise.prompt: Create a dictionary for a book with title "Orbit" and pages 120. Increase pages by 10 and print the title and updated pages.
checks: Output is Orbit then 130.
The dictionary still has exactly two keys.
A missing optional author can be read with book.get("author", "Unknown").

quiz.question: Which collection maps a task name to its duration?
quiz.explanation: A dictionary stores key/value associations and retrieves a duration using its task-name key.

lessons.title: 6. Repeat work with loops
lessons.takeaway: Loops process each item and accumulate results.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A for loop iterates over items in a sequence or other iterable. range(3) produces 0, 1, and 2; its stop is excluded. An accumulator starts at a neutral value such as 0 and is updated during each iteration.

A while loop repeats while a condition remains true. It is useful when the number of repetitions is unknown, but the body must eventually make the condition false. break exits a loop and continue skips the remainder of the current iteration.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: This loop includes only study sessions that last at least 20 minutes. The list comprehension expresses the same filtering when a new list is useful. Keep an ordinary loop when there are several actions or complex logic.
sections.example:
sessions = [10, 25, 30]
total = 0
for minutes in sessions:
    if minutes >= 20:
        total += minutes
print(total)
print([m for m in sessions if m >= 20])

# Expected output:
# 55
# [25, 30]

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Resetting total inside the loop discards earlier work. Avoid removing list items while iterating over that same list; build a new filtered list. Watch for infinite while loops whose counters never change.

exercise.prompt: Given [2, 5, 8, 11], compute the sum of even numbers with a for loop.
checks: Output is 10.
An empty list prints 0.
A list of only odd numbers prints 0.

quiz.question: What values are produced by range(1, 4)?
quiz.explanation: The start is included and the stop is excluded.

lessons.title: 7. Write reusable functions
lessons.takeaway: A function turns inputs into an explicit result.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: def defines a function with parameters: names for its inputs. Calling the function supplies arguments. return sends a result to the caller and ends that call. A function that reaches the end without return produces None.

Variables created inside a function are usually local to that call. Prefer passing data in and returning data out instead of changing global variables. This makes the function easier to reuse and test. A short docstring can explain its contract.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The function computes minutes from a number of sessions, and a default argument supplies a usual session length. Printing remains outside the calculation, so another caller could save or compare the returned number.
sections.example:
def study_minutes(sessions, length=25):
    """Return total minutes for equally long sessions."""
    return sessions * length

print(study_minutes(3))
print(study_minutes(2, length=15))

# Expected output:
# 75
# 30

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Printing a number does not return it. Avoid mutable defaults such as items=[] because the same list can be reused across calls; use None and create a list inside the function. Name parameters consistently and distinguish a function definition from a function call.

exercise.prompt: Write rectangle_area(width, height) returning the product. Call it for 4 by 3 and for 0 by 7.
exercise.solution:
def rectangle_area(width, height):
    return width * height

print(rectangle_area(4, 3))
print(rectangle_area(0, 7))
checks: Output is 12 then 0.
The function returns a value without printing inside it.
rectangle_area(3, 4) also returns 12.

quiz.question: What is the result of a function with no return statement?
quiz.explanation: Python returns None when execution reaches the end without an explicit return value.

lessons.title: 8. Read errors and validate input
lessons.takeaway: Handle expected failures specifically and let unexpected bugs remain visible.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A syntax error means Python could not parse the program. An exception occurs while a valid program runs, such as converting "abc" to an integer. Read the exception type and message, then find the relevant line in the traceback.

try contains an operation that may fail; except names the failure you know how to handle. raise reports a violated rule. Validation establishes a function contract before the rest of the program uses the data.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: parse_minutes handles a conversion error and rejects negative values. The caller catches ValueError and gives a useful message. Valid input and invalid input are deliberately tried in the same example.

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: A bare except can hide programming errors and interrupt signals. Catch a narrow type near the operation you understand. Do not return a fake success value after a failure; the caller should be able to distinguish valid zero minutes from invalid input.

exercise.prompt: Write parse_count(text) that accepts whole numbers of 1 or more and raises ValueError for zero or negative values. Demonstrate "3" and "0".
checks: Output is 3 then count must be positive.
"abc" also raises ValueError from int.
"1" is accepted; do not reject the lower valid boundary.

quiz.question: Which exception should you catch around int("abc")?
quiz.explanation: ValueError describes a value unsuitable for the requested conversion. A narrow handler preserves unrelated failures.

lessons.title: 9. Save files and structured data
lessons.takeaway: Use explicit encoding and JSON to persist ordinary records.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A file stores data after the process ends. pathlib.Path describes a filesystem path. read_text and write_text work with text; specify encoding="utf-8" so behavior is consistent across machines. A relative path is resolved from the current working directory.

JSON represents objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. json.dumps converts supported Python values to JSON text; json.loads reads JSON text into Python values. Saving and loading are separate operations, and loaded data still needs validation.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: This example uses a temporary directory so it does not overwrite your own files. It writes a small session record, reads it back, and prints the recovered fields. In your project, choose a deliberate data path.
sections.example:
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import json

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder) / "sessions.json"
    path.write_text(json.dumps({"topic": "loops", "minutes": 25}), encoding="utf-8")
    saved = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    print(saved["topic"])
    print(saved["minutes"])

# Expected output:
# loops
# 25

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Writing a file replaces its previous contents. Do not use a valuable existing file for experiments. JSON object keys become strings, and JSON does not automatically preserve custom classes or tuples. A missing file raises FileNotFoundError and broken JSON raises json.JSONDecodeError; these are different recovery cases.

exercise.prompt: Round-trip a list containing "read" and "code" through a temporary tasks.json file. Print the recovered list length and first item.
exercise.starter:
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import json
# Write, read, and inspect a list
exercise.solution:
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import json

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder) / "tasks.json"
    path.write_text(json.dumps(["read", "code"]), encoding="utf-8")
    tasks = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    print(len(tasks))
    print(tasks[0])
checks: Output is 2 then read.
The JSON file contains an array, not Python source.
Repeat with an empty list and verify the length is 0 before indexing.

quiz.question: What does json.loads need as its input?
quiz.explanation: loads parses JSON text; load is the related function that reads from a file-like object.

lessons.title: 10. Modules and project environments
lessons.takeaway: Separate reusable code and select the interpreter intentionally.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A module is a Python file whose definitions can be imported. A package groups modules. Standard library modules ship with Python, while third-party packages require separate installation. Avoid naming your files json.py, unittest.py, or other library names.

A virtual environment gives a project its own interpreter context and installed packages. Create one with python -m venv .venv. On Windows call .venv\Scripts\python.exe directly; on macOS/Linux call .venv/bin/python. Direct invocation avoids shell activation differences. Use that interpreter with -m pip when installing a needed dependency.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The runnable example uses only the standard library. For a two-file project, put your function in helpers.py, then import it from main.py in the same folder. The guard if __name__ == "__main__": limits script entry code to direct execution, keeping imports from unexpectedly running the program.

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Installing into one interpreter and running another causes confusing missing-module errors. Inspect sys.executable to see which interpreter is active. Keep .venv out of version control and document dependencies; do not copy an environment between machines. No third-party installation is needed for this path.

exercise.prompt: Write format_label(topic, minutes) in helpers.py and import it in main.py. For a quick one-file check, use the solution below; then split the definition and the call into the two files.
exercise.starter:
# helpers.py: define format_label
# main.py: import and call it
checks: One-file output is functions: 20 min.
After splitting files, python main.py gives the same output.
Importing helpers in the interactive prompt does not print anything.
Run the program with the virtual environment interpreter and inspect sys.executable.

quiz.question: Which command ties pip to the selected Python interpreter?
options: Any pip command always selects the right project
quiz.explanation: The -m form runs pip as a module of that interpreter. Substitute your virtual environment interpreter path for python.

lessons.title: 11. Test behavior and understand APIs
lessons.takeaway: Separate data processing from external I/O so it can be checked offline.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A test states an expected behavior for an input. Start with a normal case, an empty case, and an invalid or boundary case. unittest.TestCase supplies assertions and a runner in the standard library; a test failure should identify a behavior worth investigating.

An HTTP API is a remote service accepting requests and returning responses. A response has a status, headers, and body. JSON is one common body format. Networks can time out, services can reject requests, and returned data can differ from what you expected; HTTP success alone does not prove a usable schema.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The example processes an API-shaped JSON fixture entirely offline and tests the same parser. Real retrieval could use urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10) in a with block followed by json.load(response). Keep the URL configured, inspect service documentation, handle HTTPError/URLError, and validate the decoded data before passing it to your calculation.
sections.example:
import json
import unittest

def total_minutes(payload):
    return sum(item["minutes"] for item in payload["sessions"])

class TotalTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_empty(self):
        self.assertEqual(total_minutes({"sessions": []}), 0)

suite = unittest.defaultTestLoader.loadTestsFromTestCase(TotalTests)
result = unittest.TestResult()
suite.run(result)
print(f"Tests passed: {result.wasSuccessful()}")
payload = json.loads('{"sessions":[{"minutes":15},{"minutes":20}]}')
print(total_minutes(payload))

# Expected output:
# Tests passed: True
# 35

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: A test that only prints a value does not check it. Keep a unit test deterministic: do not depend on a live service staying available. Never place API keys in source or publish them; load credentials from environment variables when a real service needs them. Retrying writes can duplicate actions, so learn the API semantics before retrying.

exercise.prompt: Write count_completed(tasks) for records with a boolean done field. Test an empty list and a list with one completed and one incomplete task. Use unittest assertions, then print the number of passing tests.
exercise.starter:
import unittest
def count_completed(tasks):
    pass
# Add two tests
checks: Output is 2 then True.
Temporarily change the expected mixed result to 2; success becomes False.
Restore the correct expectation after proving the test can fail.
Explain which fields a real API response must provide before this function can use it.

quiz.question: Why use a saved JSON fixture in a unit test?
options: It guarantees the real API never changes
It makes parsing checks deterministic without a network dependency
It removes the need to validate real responses
quiz.explanation: A fixed fixture isolates your parsing behavior. Separate integration checks are needed for a real service.

lessons.title: 12. Capstone: a persistent study log
lessons.takeaway: Combine validation, functions, storage, and checks into a useful small program.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Build a study log that stores records with a topic and nonnegative whole minutes, and reports total minutes. Plan the data format and functions before writing the terminal interface: validate a record, add it to a list, save/load the list, and summarize it.

Keep this first version small. A list of dictionaries is enough; a class is optional, not a requirement. A class would bundle state and methods into objects, useful when behavior grows, but dictionaries and functions make the current contract easy to inspect.

sections.title: Work through an example
paragraphs: The example adds two validated records, saves them in a temporary folder, reloads them, and summarizes the result. The practical exercise extends the program with a topic summary. A real CLI could use argparse for commands such as add and summary; learn that module after the core functions work.
sections.example:
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import json

def add_session(log, topic, minutes):
    if not isinstance(topic, str) or not topic.strip():
        raise ValueError("topic is required")
    if type(minutes) is not int or minutes < 0:
        raise ValueError("minutes must be a nonnegative integer")
    log.append({"topic": topic.strip(), "minutes": minutes})

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    log = []
    add_session(log, "Python", 25)
    add_session(log, "Python", 15)
    path = Path(folder) / "study.json"
    path.write_text(json.dumps(log, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    restored = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    print(f"Sessions: {len(restored)}")
    print(f"Minutes: {sum(s['minutes'] for s in restored)}")

# Expected output:
# Sessions: 2
# Minutes: 40

sections.title: Avoid a common mistake
paragraphs: Do not silently overwrite malformed data with an empty log. Report JSON or schema errors and keep the file for recovery. Concurrent writers and interrupted writes require more careful storage; this beginner version is for one local process. Before using a permanent file, back it up and add tests for invalid records.

exercise.prompt: Extend the log with totals_by_topic(log), returning a dictionary of accumulated minutes per topic. Use Python 25, Reading 10, and Python 15 as the sample. Then integrate it with lesson 9 storage and lesson 11 tests.
checks: Output is {'Python': 40, 'Reading': 10}.
An empty log returns {}.
Two records with the same topic add instead of replacing the earlier minutes.
Save and reload the sample log; totals stay the same.
Add tests proving blank topics, negative minutes, and True as minutes are rejected by add_session.
Explain an intentional limitation: one process, local file storage, no account system.

quiz.question: What should happen when an existing log contains malformed JSON?
options: Report the error and preserve the file for recovery
Treat it as a successful empty log
quiz.explanation: A parse failure does not mean the user has no data. Preserve the file and make the failure visible.
